> x = (−1)^sign · (1.m₂₂m₂₁...m₀) · 2^(e − bias)

The rule is precise and binary:

| Exponent field value | Classification | Implied leading bit |
|---|---|---|
| `00000000` (all zeros) | **Denormalized** | `0.` |
| `00000001` through `11111110` | **Normalized** | `1.` |
| `11111111` (all ones) | `NaN` / `Inf` | — |

So the test is simply: if the raw 8-bit exponent field equals **zero**, the number is denormalized and the mantissa is interpreted as `0.m₂₂m₂₁...m₀`. Otherwise, it is normalized and the mantissa is interpreted as `1.m₂₂m₂₁...m₀`. [1](ass1_p1.pdf)

Think of writing a recipe versus actually cooking the meal. Writing the recipe down does not produce any food — you still have to take it to the kitchen and cook it.

In C, `code hello.c` is like **writing the recipe**. It simply opens your file in the editor so you can type your instructions. It does not compile or run anything.

To actually produce output, you need two more steps after you have saved your file:

```
make hello
./hello
```

`make hello` is the **compiler** — it reads your C source code and turns it into an executable program. `./hello` is what actually **runs** that program and produces output in the terminal. [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2025/notes/1/)
